title: Strength returned
hook: strength has come, bonds are broken; tradition hears this as the young Gobind's answer (Salok 54, ang 1429)

segments.voice: Yesterday: strength gone, and your line: only you. Did you ask for help with one thing you'd been carrying alone? Today the very next salok answers yesterday's, almost word for word. Day six hundred five.

Picture a letter arriving from a prison. Inside, a father has written two lines: my strength is gone, I'm in chains, nothing works. Now picture the reply, written by his son, who is about nine years old. Sikh tradition tells exactly this story. It says that Guru Tegh Bahadur, held in Delhi, sent yesterday's salok to Anandpur as a kind of question, and that the young Gobind Rai, who would become Guru Gobind Singh, sent back an answer in the same meter, line for line. Whatever history finally says about how it happened, the two saloks sit next to each other in the Guru Granth Sahib, and they read like a call and a reply. Today: strength returned.
screen: `A LETTER FROM A PRISON.` → `A REPLY FROM A NINE-YEAR-OLD.` → `A CALL AND AN ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Put them side by side. Salok fifty-three said bal chhutkio: strength has slipped away. Salok fifty-four, on the same Ang, fourteen twenty-nine, says bal hoaa: strength has come. Fifty-three said bandhan pare: the bonds have fallen on me. Fifty-four says bandhan chhute: the bonds are broken. Fifty-three said nothing works. Fifty-four, in paraphrase, says everything is possible. And then the second line: Nanak, all is in Your hands; You alone are the helper. Notice what didn't change. Both saloks end in the same place: God as the help. In fifty-three, the speaker leans on God because his own strength is gone. In fifty-four, the strength is back, and it's still God's. The return of strength doesn't become a reason for pride. That's the quiet lesson in the pair. We tend to pray when things are bad and forget when they're good. These two lines hold both seasons to the same shelter. A word about the history. The salok is printed among Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks, and scholars differ on who composed it. Many Sikhs follow the tradition that it was the young Gobind's reply; others read it as the ninth Guru's own answer to his own question. The text doesn't settle it. What's certain is what came next in the story Sikhs tell: the father went to his death in Delhi in 1675, and the boy grew up to found the Khalsa. A child who could answer chains with strength returned. That's how the tradition remembers him.
screen: `STRENGTH GONE; STRENGTH COME.` · `BONDS FALLEN; BONDS BROKEN.` · `BOTH END IN THE SAME SHELTER.` · `WHO WROTE IT: SCHOLARS DIFFER.` · then, large: `ALL IS IN YOUR HANDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: encourage someone stuck. Sit and think of one person you know who is in yesterday's salok right now: worn out, tangled up, nothing working. Picture their face. Then picture what an answer might sound like, the way the reply answered the letter. Not advice, not a lecture. A few words that hand some strength back. Maybe: I'm with you. Maybe: you've got more in you than you think. If you pray, you can hold them in your mind and say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Strength returned. Bal hoaa, bandhan chhute: strength has come, the bonds are broken, and it all still rests in God's hands.
Your line: all is in your hands. Send the person you pictured a short message today, a few words that hand some strength back. Day six hundred five.

howItsDone: Sikhs read saloks fifty-three and fifty-four together at the close of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and many tell the story of the father's letter and the son's reply when they do.

myth: saloks fifty-three and fifty-four sit side by side on the same Ang
both are on Ang 1429, and they read like a call and a reply.
in salok fifty-four, returned strength becomes a reason for pride
it ends where fifty-three ended: all is in Your hands, You are the helper.
everyone agrees who composed salok fifty-four

fork.setup: you're nine. your father writes from prison: my strength is gone, nothing works. what does the reply in tradition say?
options: strength has come, the bonds are broken; all is in Your hands.
fork.reveal: the reply turns every phrase of the call around, and still ends with God as the helper.

original.note: Gurmukhi: sahaai, helper; both saloks end with God as the one who helps.

trapdoor: what you thought: strength returned means you've done it yourself now.
what it means: strength is back, and it's still held in God's hands.
what a scholar hears: salok 54 mirrors 53 phrase by phrase (bal chhutkio / bal hoaa; bandhan pare / bandhan chhute); its authorship is debated, with a strong tradition naming the young Gobind Rai.

sources.ref: Salok Mahalla 9, saloks 53–54 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1429)

notes: Transliteration bal hoaa bandhan chhute sabh kichh hot upaai / naanak sabh kichh tumrai haath mai tum hee hot sahaai: confirm.
Authorship of salok 54 is debated (tradition: Guru Gobind Singh's reply; others: Guru Tegh Bahadur). Keeper to confirm the even-handed wording.
Gobind Rai's age in 1675 given as about nine (born 1666): confirm.
